newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir militants seek say in India-Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir militants seek say in India-Pakistan talks.

text.p: Separatist leaders from the disputed Himalayan territory of Kashmir on Thursday demanded a role in talks between India and Pakistan.

Top-level talks between the two nations are scheduled to start in New Delhi on Friday. No agenda has been announced for the four-day discussions in the Indian capital, but Pakistan insists Kashmir is the "core issue".

"The state of Jammu and Kashmir is not an integral part of India or Pakistan. Jammu and Kashmir belongs to its people. They are the principal party and should be involved in any talks on its future," Omar Farooq, chairman of Kashmir's umbrella All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, told a news conference.
The last round of India-Pakistan talks in 1994 broke down over Kashmir. India controls two-thirds of the Himalayan territory and Pakistan the rest.
The two neighbours have gone to war twice over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947.
Jammu and Kashmir is mainly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state. Pakistan calls the territory it controls Azad (Free) Kashmir.

The Hurriyat bands some 30 religious and political groups which want a plebiscite in Kashmir that Pakistan, citing U.N. resolutions, has long sought. India wants the dispute to be resolved bilaterally under a 1972 accord.
Farooq said the dispute over Kashmir had festered for 50 years because its people were not consulted about its future.

"The people of Jammu and Kashmir will resist any attempt at striking a deal between India and Pakistan. It will be construed as a blatant mockery of the agony of the people of Jammu and Kashmir," he said.

Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have died since a separatist insurgency erupted in Kashmir in 1990. India charges that Pakistan arms and trains the Moslem rebels, but Islamabad denies this.
